questions.question: [Energy Stores and Transfers] Foundation Name the eight energy stores and give one example of each.
questions.correctAnswer: Kinetic — moving car; gravitational potential — book on shelf; elastic potential — stretched spring; thermal — hot cup of tea; chemical — food/fuel; nuclear — uranium in reactor; magnetic — two repelling magnets held apart; electrostatic — two opposite charges separated.
questions.explanation: Kinetic — moving car; gravitational potential — book on shelf; elastic potential — stretched spring; thermal — hot cup of tea; chemical — food/fuel; nuclear — uranium in reactor; magnetic — two repelling magnets held apart; electrostatic — two opposite charges separated.

questions.question: [Energy Stores and Transfers] Foundation A ball falls from a height of 2 m. Describe the energy transfers that take place.
questions.correctAnswer: At the top: gravitational potential store is at its maximum, kinetic store is zero. As the ball falls: gravitational potential store decreases, kinetic store increases. questions.question: [Energy Stores and Transfers] Foundation State the conservation of energy principle.
questions.correctAnswer: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred usefully, stored, or dissipated. The total energy input always equals the total energy output.
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred usefully, stored, or dissipated. The total energy input always equals the total energy output.

questions.question: [Particle Motion and Pressure] Foundation Describe what causes gas pressure in a sealed container.
questions.correctAnswer: Gas particles are in constant random motion. They collide with the walls of the container, exerting a force on them. The total force per unit area of the wall is the gas pressure.
questions.explanation: Gas particles are in constant random motion. They collide with the walls of the container, exerting a force on them. The total force per unit area of the wall is the gas pressure.

questions.question: [Particle Motion and Pressure] Foundation Explain how Brownian motion provides evidence for the particle model.
questions.correctAnswer: Brownian motion shows larger particles (e.g. smoke) moving in random zigzag paths. This is caused by collisions with smaller, invisible air or water particles. This random, uneven bombardment can only be explained if matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion — supporting the particle model
questions.explanation: Brownian motion shows larger particles (e.g. smoke) moving in random zigzag paths. This is caused by collisions with smaller, invisible air or water particles. This random, uneven bombardment can only be explained if matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion — supporting the particle model

questions.question: [Particle Motion and Pressure] Higher A gas at 150 kPa has a volume of 4.0 m³. The volume is reduced to 1.5 m³ at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure.
[Nuclear Model and Isotopes] Foundation Describe the results of Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment and what each result tells us about the structure of the atom.
questions.correctAnswer: Most alpha particles went straight through → the atom is mostly empty space. Some were deflected → the nucleus is positively charged. A few bounced back → the nucleus is small, dense and contains most of the mass.
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles went straight through → the atom is mostly empty space. Some were deflected → the nucleus is positively charged. A few bounced back → the nucleus is small, dense and contains most of the mass.

questions.question: [Nuclear Model and Isotopes] Foundation An atom has 26 protons and 30 neutrons. State its atomic number and mass number.
questions.correctAnswer: Atomic number = 26 (number of protons). Mass number = 26 + 30 = 56 (protons + neutrons). This is iron-56.
questions.explanation: Atomic number = 26 (number of protons). Mass number = 26 + 30 = 56 (protons + neutrons). This is iron-56.

questions.question: [Nuclear Model and Isotopes] Higher Explain what isotopes are, using carbon-12 and carbon-14 as examples.
questions.correctAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. They are both carbon (atomic number 6) but have different mass numbers (12 and 14).
questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. They are both carbon (atomic number 6) but have different mass numbers (12 and 14).

questions.question: [Nuclear Model and Isotopes] Describe how and why our model of the atom has changed from Dalton's solid sphere to the nuclear model. Include the evidence that led to each change. [6 marks] <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Dalton proposed the solid sphere model, suggesting atoms were tiny indivisible spheres (1). Thomson discovered the electron in 1897, showing atoms contained smaller negatively charged particles, so he proposed the plum pudding model — a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded within it (1).
